catalog_quote: A detailed analysis of stress in Marri Ngarr is beyond the scope of this thesis; however here I make some basic generalisations about word stress. Note that these findings are impressionistic and further investigation is required for a more comprehensive understanding of the stress system in Marri Ngarr. In nominals, primary stress occurs on the first syllable of the stem. Words with three or more syllables can attract secondary stress on the third syllable. /ŋáta/ ‘house’ /málaŋ/ ‘Brolga’ ... /wádiwàŋ/ ‘male Antilopine wallaroo’ ... Procliticisation does not affect stress placement. ... In simple verbs, stress generally falls on the first syllable of the classifier stem (35). Secondary stress is generally attracted to the third syllable of the verb (36), provided this is not a tense enclitic. Note that stress can be attracted to an epenthetic vowel. ... In bipartite verbs, primary stress generally falls on the first syllable of the lexical stem, while secondary stress falls on the initial syllable of the classifier stem, so long as it is not adjacent to a stressed syllable (37) - (38). ... The examples in (39) - (41) below show that it is the classifier stem and lexical stem in particular that attract stress, rather than stress assignment being based on syllable timing.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the stem: for nominals the first syllable of the nominal stem (proclitics such as anim a= are ignored); for simple verbs the first syllable of the classifier stem; for bipartite verbs the first syllable of the lexical stem (with the classifier stem taking secondary stress). The pattern is stem-initial and morphologically anchored rather than counted from the phonological word edge, which is why it is read as morphologically determined rather than fixed: initial syllable; in isolated nominals it surfaces as initial stress. Examples: /ŋáta/ 'house', /málaŋ/ 'Brolga', /wádiwàŋ/ 'male Antilopine wallaroo', /a=címbec/.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nominals: secondary stress on the third syllable in words of three or more syllables (/wádiwàŋ/). Simple verbs: secondary on the third syllable of the verb provided it is not a tense enclitic; stress can land on an epenthetic vowel. Bipartite verbs: secondary on the initial syllable of the classifier stem so long as it is not adjacent to a stressed syllable; stress placement tracks the stems, not syllable count (exx. 39-41). Reduplicated nominals and reduplicated lexical stems stress both copies (/wúkwúk/, /márimári/).
new_statements.exceptions: Some animal terms with a reanalysed anim classifier take secondary stress on the classifier vowel and primary stress on the third syllable, attributed to heavy second syllables (/à=kalémbi/ 'Water rat', /à=jilírki/ 'meat', /à=βijélmbu/ 'Kookaburra'). Disyllabic lexical stems occasionally take primary stress on their second syllable (ex. 42, fn. 19). Unlike Marrithiyel and Ngan'gityemerri, stress does not fall on applicatives and generally not on incorporated body parts, though ex. (48) is an exception. Author states the generalisations are impressionistic.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: phonological/grammatical word (nominal stem, simple verb, bipartite verb), with clitics explicitly excluded from the stress domain; based on transcribed recordings (1972 Green/Walsh tapes and later fieldwork), not instrumental.
new_statements.identity_note: Bicevskis 2023 describes Marri Ngarr (= Glottolog Maringarr mari1419; Tryon's 'Marengar'), the language of the Moyle River / Wadeye area, from a corpus of recordings 1972-2020s. No dialect split is made; the description is of the language as a whole.

sources.note: §2.2.3 Stress (pp. 34-38): nominals take primary stress on the first syllable of the stem, secondary on the third syllable in 3+ syllable words; proclitics (anim a=) do not shift stress; some animal terms with reanalysed classifier show secondary on the classifier vowel and primary on the (heavy) third syllable; reduplicated nominals stress both copies; simple verbs stress first syllable of the classifier stem with secondary on the third syllable (not on tense enclitics); bipartite verbs: primary on first syllable of the lexical stem, secondary on first syllable of the classifier stem unless…
